title: The Predator Principle — The Cancer of Evolution · Nirodha Collective

items.title: Science must test the metaphors it inherited
items.content_text:
We suspect that scientific and popular corpora make competition and extraction more visible than symbiosis, cooperation, and conflict control.

This is not an accusation against researchers. It is a testable question: preregistered dictionaries, blinded annotation, multiple disciplines, multiple languages, and publication even if the result is null.



Evidence boundary: Hypothesis: systematic overweighting has not yet been demonstrated.

items.title: Does the biosphere carry a memory of pressure?
items.content_text:
We propose a research model connecting chronic threat, stress effects, reproductive loss, behavioural contraction, disrupted interaction networks, and industrial extraction.

If this model explains or predicts nothing beyond existing indicators, the term is scientifically unnecessary. That test is what makes it serious.



Evidence boundary: Not a clinical diagnosis of Earth; the construct's added value is unproven.

items.title: Earth is not a warehouse
items.content_text:
Human land use, biomass redistribution, and appropriation of biological production operate at planetary scale. Modern extraction exceeds the reach of a local predator-prey relation.

The Predator Principle therefore asks not only how much is taken. It asks whether those carrying the harm can return effective feedback to the decision.



Evidence boundary: Planetary changes have multiple causes and are not explained by predation alone.

items.title: Humans hunt differently
items.content_text:
Humans often remove adult animals and therefore reproductive capital. In compared systems, human exploitation rates reached up to 14 times those of other predators.

This does not make every human a morally guilty predator. It reveals an unusual ecological signature that technology and markets can scale dramatically.



Evidence boundary: Results differ across fisheries, hunting, regions, and management regimes.

items.title: The threat does not end when the predator leaves
items.content_text:
An experiment in wild animals found PTSD-like changes in behaviour, the amygdala, and the hippocampus persisting for at least seven days after predator cues.

This does not prove trauma of the entire Earth. It shows that the nonlethal effects of severe threat can be biologically real and extended in time.



Evidence boundary: PTSD-like denotes measured analogies, not a human clinical diagnosis of the animal.

items.title: The strongest objection to our thesis
items.content_text:
Keystone predators can maintain diversity, and the loss of large predators can trigger trophic cascades. This research belongs at the centre of any honest critique of the Predator Principle.

Our answer is not denial. We distinguish an ecologically embedded interaction from a detached organising principle that privatises gains and leaves harm to the larger system.



Evidence boundary: Predator effects are context-dependent; they can stabilise or destabilise.

items.title: Complexity did not arise through struggle alone
items.content_text:
Genes became genomes, cells became organisms, and organisms formed cooperative groups. Such transitions stabilise when parts cooperate and conflict within the new whole is controlled.

Competition does not disappear. But without cooperation and conflict control, durable higher-level individuality does not emerge.



Evidence boundary: Cooperation alone does not guarantee stability; competition remains part of evolutionary processes.

items.title: Predators act even when they do not kill
items.content_text:
In a controlled field experiment, songbirds exposed to perceived predation risk produced 40 percent fewer offspring even though the experimental effect operated through fear rather than additional killing.

The costs of predation therefore extend beyond consumed bodies. They can alter reproduction, foraging, movement, and attention.



Evidence boundary: A single empirical result in songbirds; not a universal effect size for all species.

items.title: Five signs that a system is becoming predatory
items.content_text:
One-way resource flow. Externalised harm. Ineffective dissent. Compulsory escalation. Destruction of the common foundation.

Our hypothesis is attackable: when at least four characteristics persist together, local optimisation increasingly risks instability at the next system level.



Evidence boundary: This four-of-five threshold is a systems hypothesis that requires validation.

items.title: A predator is not a model for the future
items.content_text:
Predation exists and can perform functions in present ecosystems. This creates no obligation to copy its logic into economies, politics, or artificial intelligence.

The Predator Principle begins when extraction externalises harm, disables correction, compels escalation, and damages the shared substrate. What wins locally can make the larger system lose.



Evidence boundary: Interpretation: ecological predation and the defined system pattern are not identical.
